subject: geography
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: How many figures are in an Ordnance Survey grid reference that locates a point to the nearest 100 metres?
questions.explain: A six-figure grid reference pinpoints a location to the nearest 100 m, whereas a four-figure reference only identifies a whole 1 km grid square.

questions.q: When reading an OS grid reference, which coordinate is quoted first?
questions.explain: The rule is 'along the corridor, then up the stairs' - eastings (the horizontal figure) are always read before northings.

questions.q: On an OS map, what does a pattern of contour lines drawn very close together indicate?
questions.explain: Closely spaced contours mean the land rises or falls sharply over a short distance, so the gradient is steep.

questions.q: On a 1:50 000 OS map, how much real distance does a straight-line measurement of 2 cm represent?
questions.explain: At 1:50 000, 1 cm represents 500 m, so 2 cm represents 1 000 m, which is 1 km.

questions.q: On a 1:25 000 OS map, a footpath measures 6 cm. What is its real length?
questions.explain: At 1:25 000, 1 cm represents 250 m, so 6 cm represents 1 500 m, which is 1.5 km.

questions.q: Which type of map uses graded shading or colour to show the density or amount of a variable across different areas?
questions.explain: A choropleth map shows spatial variation by shading regions, with darker or denser shading representing higher values.

questions.q: What does a line on an isoline map represent?
options: Points that all have the same value
The direction of movement of goods
A route of equal walking time
questions.explain: Isolines join together all points of equal value, such as contours (height) or isotherms (temperature).

questions.q: On a flow-line map, what does the width of each arrow usually represent?
options: The volume or amount of movement
questions.explain: On a flow-line map wider arrows show larger volumes of movement, such as more people or greater trade flows.

questions.q: Which graph is most appropriate for showing the relationship between two variables to see if they are correlated?
questions.explain: A scatter graph plots paired values as points, making any correlation (positive, negative or none) between the two variables visible.

questions.q: In a set of data, what is the 'median'?
options: The middle value when the data are placed in order
The sum of the values divided by how many there are
The difference between the highest and lowest value
questions.explain: The median is the central value once all data are arranged in rank order, so half the values lie above it and half below.

questions.q: Which measure of central tendency is the value that occurs most often in a data set?
questions.explain: The mode is simply the most frequently occurring value in a set of data.

questions.q: The 'range' of a data set is calculated by...
options: subtracting the lowest value from the highest value
adding all the values and dividing by the number of values
questions.explain: The range measures the spread of data and is found by taking the smallest value away from the largest.

questions.q: What is the mean of the values 4, 8, 10 and 6?
questions.explain: The mean is the total (4 + 8 + 10 + 6 = 28) divided by the number of values (4), which gives 7.

questions.q: How is the interquartile range calculated?
questions.explain: The interquartile range shows the spread of the middle 50% of ordered data and equals the upper quartile minus the lower quartile.

questions.q: Spearman's rank correlation coefficient is used to measure...
options: the strength and direction of a relationship between two sets of data
the average value of a data set
the total amount of a variable
questions.explain: Spearman's rank produces a value between +1 and -1 that shows how strongly two ranked variables are correlated and whether the correlation is positive or negative.

questions.q: A town's population rose from 20 000 to 25 000. What is the percentage increase?
questions.explain: Percentage change is the change (5 000) divided by the original value (20 000), multiplied by 100, giving 25%.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of primary data collected during fieldwork?
options: Pedestrian counts you carried out yourself in a street
Population figures downloaded from the census website
A newspaper article about the area
A textbook description of the coastline
questions.explain: Primary data is information collected first-hand by the investigator, such as your own counts, measurements or questionnaires.

questions.q: In sampling, what is 'systematic sampling'?
options: Selecting data at regular intervals, such as every 10th person or every 50 m
Deliberately choosing sites the investigator finds interesting
Dividing the population into groups and sampling each in proportion
questions.explain: Systematic sampling collects data at fixed, regular intervals, giving even coverage across a site or population.

questions.q: Which statement best describes qualitative data?
options: Descriptive information such as opinions, field sketches or photographs
Data that can only be shown as numbers
questions.explain: Qualitative data describes qualities and views rather than measurable amounts, for example interview responses or annotated photographs.

questions.q: What is the usual first stage of a geographical fieldwork enquiry?
options: Deciding on a question, aim or hypothesis to investigate
Evaluating the reliability of the results
questions.explain: An enquiry begins by identifying a suitable question, aim or hypothesis, which then guides the data that need to be collected.
